text: Welcome to Chapter Five. So far this course has compared plain SQL statements across platforms — select, pagination, joins. Now we turn to something bigger: the procedural layer each platform bolts onto standard SQL so you can write variables, loops, conditionals, and reusable routines. Plain SQL is declarative, you describe the result you want. Procedural SQL is not — and every platform's version of it looks genuinely different.

Start with T-SQL, because you already know it. Declare at total, decimal ten two, equals zero. Select at total equals sum of list price from production dot product where product line equals R. If at total is greater than one hundred thousand, print high value product line. Notice what's missing here: no begin, no end, no enclosing block of any kind. T-SQL lets you write declare and if directly in a loose batch, which is exactly why nothing in this course's earlier chapters needed to introduce a separate block structure before using a variable.

Oracle's PL/SQL looks related but is structured very differently. Declare, then a strict declare section — v underscore total, number ten two — then begin, select sum of list price into v underscore total from products where product line equals R, if v underscore total greater than one hundred thousand then dbms output dot put line. PL/SQL is genuinely richer than T-SQL: packages, strongly typed records, far more capable exception handling. Structurally it has more in common with Ada than with T-SQL's looser batch style.

MySQL takes the opposite approach from T-SQL: procedural logic only exists inside a stored program's begin-end body. Create procedure check product line, begin, declare total decimal ten two, select sum of list price into total from products where product line equals R, if total greater than one hundred thousand then select the message, end if, end. You cannot run a loose declare or if outside a routine the way T-SQL allows. MySQL's procedural feature set has historically lagged the other three platforms, though it keeps improving release to release.

PostgreSQL is the real outlier in this comparison. It doesn't ship with one fixed procedural language at all — it supports multiple pluggable P L languages you install as extensions: P L slash p g s q l, P L slash Python, P L slash Perl, and more. In practice almost everyone uses P L slash p g s q l, Postgres's own default, deliberately modeled on Oracle's declare, begin, exception, end shape. Do dollar dollar, declare total numeric, begin, select into total, if total greater than one hundred thousand then raise notice. For the rest of this chapter, when we say PostgreSQL, we mean P L slash p g s q l.

Four platforms, four real shapes: T-SQL's loose batches, PL/SQL's Ada-like blocks, MySQL's routine-only logic, and Postgres's pluggable P L languages with P L slash p g s q l as the practical default. Next lesson, we go one level deeper and compare how each of these four actually declares and assigns variables — including a genuine surprise in MySQL, which has two completely different variable mechanisms. See you there.
